This means that the most a customer can save on a given day on a Mild tariff is less than they save on every day on the other two tariff designs (assuming a technology can shift load from the 4 highest-price hours to the four lowest-price hours in a given day). It is also notable that the residential differentials, particularly on the Full and Medium tariffs, are substantially higher than the C&I differentials, due simply to the fact that residential volumetric rates are, on average, higher than C&I rates. This can help increase residential customers’ savings potential, despite their relatively small electricity demands, but may mean that it is more challenging to pay off C&I load flexibility technologies that might scale with the size of the resource. Differences between the average of the four highest and four lowest prices in each day of the year, for the 2030 low price forecast, across customer class, utility, and tariff design scenarios. 3.2 End use load response 3.2.1 Hourly load impacts This section shows the results from the end use response model across the entire customer base. Load impacts therefore represent the technical potential of price response if 100% of customers responded and were as flexible as our models assume. Because the baseline load data is developed from 2019 meter data, the baseline for comparison is customer load on 2019 tariffs, which were largely TOU tariffs. Any load response modeled in this study is additive to the amount of TOU-driven load response observed in 2019. Results for the 2030 Low price scenario are shown. In general, Medium and Mild tariffs produce similar load response to the Full tariff, with the response of the “fully dispatchable” loads being nearly identical. Thermal loads perform slightly less price response on the Medium, and less on the Mild, tariffs due to fewer hours during which the price differential can make up for the cost of thermal losses. Average daily load shapes for each end use in 2030 (low price scenario) are shown in Figure 13. For each end use, the baseline customer demand is shown as the dashed line, then the new load after responding to the Full dynamic price is shown. The area highlighted in orange is when load was shed, while the blue area shows load that was increased. Several interesting things emerge from these figures. EV charging, pool pumps, and crop irrigation are modeled as being fully dispatchable as long as energy requirements within a given window are met, and therefore the load becomes highly concentrated in the middle of the day when prices are low. (Spa pumps are not shown but have an identical daily load shape pattern to Pool pumps at about 1/10th the total magnitude).
